        Station

        Star map

        How this works

        The loop

        Earn cr → fit a better ship → reach more dangerous space → earn faster. Mine asteroids, haul goods between stations, run missions, build things, or take what others built. When a ship dies, it and everything on it are gone forever. Keep spare ships and cr at stations.

        Flying

        Mouse steers · W/S throttle · Shift boost · Tab targets. The OVERVIEW (right panel) is your world: click a row, then Warp / Approach / Orbit. E docks or interacts · N star map · J spools a hyperspace jump along the lane to the next system (align, hold, and the stars stretch) · 1–8 cycle fitted modules. Green systems (0.5+) are policed; red ones pay better and shoot back.

        At a station

        Market trades · Fitting arms your ship within powergrid/CPU · Missions pay cr and standing · Skills train in real time even offline · Industry turns minerals and hours into hardware · Insurance softens the next loss.

        Ships are their parts

        Every ship is built from parts on a grid, and hits land on the part they strike. Lose a thruster and the ship yaws toward the dead engine under power; lose the frame that holds a wing and the wing drifts away. Heat is the real limit: reactors, drives and guns make it, and only the internal heat sinks shed it — route power to weapons to bleed it faster. Past 100% parts start failing; past 130% the crew cooks. Build and refit ships in the station Shipyard; wrecks drop salvaged parts.

        Dreadnoughts

        Kilometre-long capital ships with spinning habitat rings and a hangar you can fly into — line up with the lit bay and land on a green pad. Strip a dreadnought's heat sinks and it cooks itself. Your own dreadnought: land in its hangar, E takes the bridge, T toggles tactical view, L launches your fighter.

        Relativity

        Light is slow here (3 km/s) and gravity is real. Near a black hole or a moon, flight turns ballistic: gravity pulls, W burns along the nose, S retro, Space matches the local frame, and the green arc is the nav computer's prediction (gold when a flyby will gain speed). Deep in a black hole's well your clock runs slow — the top panel reads it as "1 hour here = N hours outside" and the whole galaxy (skills, jobs, orders, markets, structures, factions) runs at the outside rate. H holds an orbit (nose prograde, so tides compress the hull); below 3 Rs no orbit holds by itself, and every second costs propellant and heat. Long, thin hulls break in the tides. The horizon is final. Wormholes show the far side; each transit spends stability by mass — the panel says whether your fleet fits. On a dreadnought's bridge, U opens mass-driver fire control: a relativistic slug shatters moons and scars planets for good. One star is going supernova on the date on the title screen. F8 sets lensing quality.

        Wormholes and signatures

        Frontier and lawless systems hide signatures — relic sites, gas, pirate hideouts and wormholes (the star map rings systems with an open one in purple). Press P and Pulse at the widest range: every signature in the system is listed, named once the return is strong, and gets a fix on your overview. Warp to the fix, pick a tighter range, pulse again; inside the resolve distance at the tightest range it resolves into a warpable site. Fly into a wormhole and press E. Every ship can scan with its own sensors; a Probe launcher adds the 1 km range for tighter fixes. Wormholes last about three hours and have a mass limit.

        The living galaxy

        The galaxy runs without you. Press I (or the Intel button) for the feed and the state of things. Factions wage their own wars: war buying drains minerals from the aggressor's markets first — prices climb before any system falls. Fronts are fed by supply convoys that fly the jump route; shoot the haulers and the front starves. A machine plague wakes in the far lawless: it eats belts and moons, copies itself and spreads along gates and open wormholes; eaten systems are stripped for good. Kill replication hubs, crack infested moons with an RKV, collapse wormholes to seal what is beyond, and research its salvage into parts nobody else has. Megastructures go up over weeks: Dyson swarms that dim their stars, an O'Neill cylinder you can fly into, space elevators (no takeoff mass penalty on their planet), mass driver arrays. Enlist with a faction, hire mercenaries, found your own, sponsor a structure, or lead the coalition against the machine plague. In cities, the spaceport terminal has jobs, an air taxi, a sky circuit, property and a cantina.

        Planets

        Inhabited worlds show it: city lights on the night side, orbital habitats and shuttle traffic, and in core space a space elevator. Each planet's capital stands near its first landing site; smaller settlements dot some of the others (the survey card says which). Cities have a spaceport pad beside the landing zone — land on it and press E to sell ore and relics, refuel, patch the hull or buy local goods. Rooftops are solid. A city under an RKV strike stays a ruin.

        Warp to a planet, hold orbit, press E — one site is always ready — and descend. Land gently on flat ground. You start with a rover in the hold: R deploys it. Drive it (P prospects) to drill deposits, grab salvage crates, ride geyser vents for gas, clear fauna nests, and run the timed circuit through the amber rings for cr. Settlements on green worlds buy ore and artifacts on the spot. B anchors a mining outpost. Climb past 900 m to leave.

        Deflectors, power and hyperspace

        Your ship carries fore and aft deflector banks over its parts: hits drain the bank on the side they land, and only a collapsed bank lets them through to the hull. [ / ] shift strength aft / fore. Power runs in pips between engines (↑), shields (←) and weapons (→); ↓ balances them. Engines mean speed, shields mean faster deflector recovery and bigger banks, weapons mean harder bolts and cooler guns. Hunters and Concordance gunships project interdiction fields: inside one the hyperdrive will not spool, and a warp line that crosses one drops you out in it. Lawless lanes can pull you out of hyperspace short of the beacon.

        On foot

        Land, then G walks you down the ramp; walk back up it to board. Click to capture the mouse. WASD move · Shift sprint · C crouch · Space jump · V roll · RMB aim · LMB fire · G hold to aim a plasma charge, release to throw · T swap shoulder · 1/2 weapons · R class ability · E interact or drive the rover · B summons the ship to you if the ground is flat and clear. Blasters overheat instead of running dry; rocks and crates stop bolts, so crouch behind them. Your deflector soaks most of a hit before your health does. Die on foot and you wake aboard the ship; what you carried waits in a container where you fell.

        The Path

        Some people touch the Resonance. It can wake at a relic in ruins, after a brush with death, in a deep orbit around a black hole — or it was always there. Two orders will come: the Wardens of the Quiet Path and the Cinder Court of the Ember. Choose a master, walk four trials, find a heartstone alone, forge your arc blade, and face the final trial. 3 ignites a blade, Q sheathes it; hold RMB to guard and time it to send bolts back where you aim. 4–8 are powers, Tab switches path, J opens the journal on foot.

        War, squads and the open world

        Allegiance: pledge to the Concordance, the Free Reach or the Syndicates at a recruiter's office in their settlements (or from the journal), or stay independent. Service earns ranks: faction gear, vehicle requisitions, a faction hull, and up to four companions at your side. Defect in wartime and your old faction hunts you for good. Independents pay more, carry less, and take contract pay from whoever they fight for. Ground battles break out where wars reach a landing site — marked ⛨ on the star map and in the news. Land, pick a side (or stay out of it), take and hold capture points to drain the enemy's tickets; respawn at a held point or your ship. Control of orbit above the battle speeds a side's dropships and unlocks X orbital strike and N strafing runs. Leave, fight in orbit, come back: the battle waits. Vehicles: E beside a hover bike, tank, gunship, heavy walker or emplacement your side holds climbs in — WASD drive, LMB/RMB fire, Space/C climb and dive (gunship), G out. Shoot vehicles part by part: a walker that loses a leg goes down. Squad: hire companions in settlement bars, rescue them, or be assigned them by rank. Z opens orders (follow, hold, attack target, cover, regroup, ability); E revives the downed in time. Outside a large battle, a companion who bleeds out is gone — their name goes on the memorial (journal → Crew & memorial, or G in the cockpit). Loyalty follows your choices; the disloyal argue, refuse, leave — or worse. Settlements stand on temperate and toxic sites: shops, the bar, recruiter, medic, information broker, garrison, repair yard and bounty board; doors (E) lead inside. Hurting residents or the garrison raises a wanted level (★) with the owner; pay fines at a garrison, or hunters come. Quests (I): leads from brokers, bars and garrisons, and the storylines — The Long Ledger, Wells of the Reach, The Velvet Debt, and for Resonants The Hollow Choir. Choices change the endings and the galaxy. Bounties: take a contract at a board, track the target (brokers, bar talk, Sense), and press U on foot for stun — a target taken alive and carried to your ship pays far more.

        Multiplayer

        Everyone playing shares space. Pilots in your system appear with nametags — in frontier/lawless space (below 0.5) they can shoot you, and you them. The lobby on the title screen hosts co-op and versus matches.

        The hint bar above the radar always suggests your next move — the × on it (or this panel) turns it off and on.
